_what: Which countries and which trades this pipeline can be pointed at -- and which it cannot.
_why: The question 'where next' kept being answered by gut feel and market size. The filter that actually decides is a different one: first, whether cold mail to businesses is lawful there at all, and second, whether the Google profile IS the sales channel in that trade. Both live here, next to the region files that make a country scrapeable.
_not_legal_advice: The legal column names the regime and what it requires in substance. It is desk research from public sources, not reviewed by a lawyer, and it does not cover your specific case. Note also that most secondary sources on this topic are published by companies selling cold-email tools, whose bias runs towards 'this is allowed' -- so the statutes are named here and the blogs are not. Before sending into any market below, confirm it for yourself.
_the_catch_that_applies_almost_everywher: In nearly every country that permits B2B cold mail, the permission covers REGISTERED COMPANIES and not sole traders. UK PECR protects individual subscribers, which includes sole traders and partnerships. The Dutch Telecommunicatiewet exempts BV/NV/stichting but not ZZP one-person businesses. South Africa's guidance turns on writing to the legal entity rather than the natural person. And the trades this system is best at -- locksmiths, plumbers, electricians -- are disproportionately sole traders. The scrape does not know the legal form. This is the single biggest unresolved gap in the market list, and it is named here rather than buried.

countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.rule: Cold mail to corporate subscribers (Ltd, PLC, LLP) needs no prior consent, provided the sender is identified and an opt-out works.
countries.catch: Sole traders and partnerships count as individual subscribers and are NOT covered.
countries.status: running -- 4,746 locksmiths scraped, the numbers on the page come from here

countries.name: United States
countries.region_level: state, with California / New York / Texas split into counties
countries.rule: Lawful. Requires a truthful sender and subject line, a working opt-out, and a valid POSTAL ADDRESS in the footer.
countries.catch: The postal address is mandatory and the thing most often left out. Some states add their own rules on top.

countries.name: Ireland
countries.rule: To companies as in the UK, with a working opt-out.
countries.catch: Small market -- three regions hold 60% of it.

countries.name: Singapore
countries.rule: The PDPA excludes business contact information from personal data altogether, which makes Singapore one of the most permissive developed markets for B2B mail. Sender identification and opt-out still apply.
countries.catch: The same sources that say this also say collecting addresses by scraping needs its own lawful basis -- which is exactly how this pipeline gets them. That tension is unresolved.

countries.name: Hong Kong
countries.rule: Commercial mail to business addresses is permitted with clear sender identification and opt-out. Business contact data sits outside the PDPO.
countries.catch: Sender contact details must stay valid for 30 days after sending. Penalties run to HK$1m.

countries.name: France
countries.rule: B2B prospecting to a professional address runs on an opt-out basis: no prior consent needed, provided the message relates to the recipient's job, the sender is identified at first contact, and a one-click opt-out is honoured.
countries.catch: The copy has to be French. Every building block, checker and subject line in this pipeline is written in English -- this is a translation project, not a config change.

countries.name: Netherlands
countries.rule: Legal entities (BV, NV, stichting, vereniging) may be mailed without prior consent, with sender identification and a working opt-out.
countries.catch: Natural persons -- ZZP sole traders, VOF partners -- need prior consent, and Dutch trades are full of them. Copy has to be Dutch.

countries.name: Australia
countries.rule: Consent is required, but a published business address can amount to inferred consent where the message relates to the function that address is published for.
countries.catch: The inference only holds while the connection is tight. Writing to a locksmith's info@ about HIS visibility fits; the same address for a web design offer does not.
countries.status: region file built, never scraped. Extremely concentrated -- 3 states hold 60%

countries.name: New Zealand
countries.rule: As Australia, on the same inference from a published business address.
countries.catch: Small market. Auckland alone is most of it.
countries.status: region file built -- being used right now to test whether one country-wide run replaces the per-region loop

countries.name: South Africa
countries.rule: POPIA requires opt-in and has no B2B carve-out. The December 2024 guidance note carved out one narrow path: role addresses (info@, sales@) written to the legal entity rather than a named person sit outside the strictest consent requirement.
countries.catch: That path is narrow and recent, and it collapses the moment the mail is addressed to a person. Buying or renting lists is prohibited outright.

countries.name: Canada
countries.rule: Requires express or narrowly-defined implied consent BEFORE sending. A published address qualifies only under tight conditions and only for messages relevant to the role.
countries.catch: Penalties reach into the millions and the regulator enforces actively. The most attractive English-speaking market you leave alone anyway.
countries.status: region file exists, sending not recommended

_avoid.DACH: Germany, Austria, Switzerland. German UWG § 7(2) treats commercial mail without prior express consent as unreasonable harassment, and unlike the UK's PECR there is no B2B exception. Sending warning letters is itself a business model there. regions/DE.json exists from earlier work and is not a recommendation.
_avoid.opt_in_EU: Spain, Italy, Poland, Denmark, Belgium apply consumer-grade consent rules to B2B as well; several require double opt-in. Sweden is the notable exception, allowing opt-out where the mail clearly relates to the recipient's professional role.
_avoid.UAE: The RUEC requires opt-in consent for B2B, plus full business details including a UAE physical address.

_niche_test: Three properties decide whether a trade suits this machine. URGENT: it is searched for in the moment of need, not during planning. LOCAL: the provider has to travel, so the map is what gets searched. NO COMPARISON: the first usable result wins the job. A trade with all three sells through its Google profile whether it means to or not -- which is exactly what the mail is about. In a trade that runs on referral (accountants, agencies, consultants), the score measures something the recipient does not care about.

_order: Green countries first, and inside them the biggest emergency trades. The UK is running; the United States is the same legal regime at roughly ten times the size and now has a region file. Market sizes are deliberately absent -- they fall out of the first scrape, and a guessed figure is exactly the kind of claim this pipeline refuses to put in a mail.
